packets.text: If there was ever a lesson that small, kind gestures can go a long way, this group of teens from Milford, Massachusetts, certainly is a wonderful example. Earlier this week, 7-year-old Tristan Caron, who has autism, was at Urban Air Adventure Park in Bellingham with his mother, Christina, when a group of teenagers invited him to play with them. The interaction left a lasting impression on Christina, who took to social media to thank the teens for including her son. Livy Molinari, one of the teenagers, told WBZ-TV that the interaction happened when she decided to ask Tristan one question after noticing he was sitting by himself. "I said 'that's a really nice ball you have,' because he had just won a ball," she said. "I was like, 'can I hold it for a second?' And he was like, 'yeah sure.'"  A simple game of toss with Tristan turned into a 40-minute jamboree of hide-and-seek, catch and fun on the slide. "He was really excited and happy when we asked his mom if he could play with us too," said Kelsey Zozzaro, one of the teens. It was more than just laughter. Tristan's mom said it was life-changing for her son who usually gets left out. She was able to identify the teenagers through Facebook.The teens told WBZ-TV that they had no idea Tristan had autism but saw him sitting alone and wanted to include him. "We just wanted to include him and have a fun time playing around at Urban Air. And I feel really happy he felt included and as joyful as he did," said Anna Held, another one of the teens. Word of the teens' actions spread quickly around the community, something the group said they did not anticipate but are embracing. "It's nice we included him and other people get to know about this, so maybe they can think about it when other people aren't included," said Kenny Leite, a teen from the group. Urban Air Adventure Park has been in contact with everyone involved and said they plan to invite everyone back to the park for a day of celebrating the teens' act of kindness.

packets.text:
A group of Milford teenagers noticed a 7-year-old boy sitting alone at Urban Air Adventure Park in Bellingham and decided to invite him to play, sparking a 40-minute session of catch, hide-and-seek, and slides that the boy's mother later called out publicly for its kindness. Teen Anna Hele said she felt happy Tristan Caron felt included.

The spontaneous interaction began when teen Livy Molinari asked Tristan about a prize ball he had won, according to CBS News Boston. That simple icebreaker quickly turned into an extended play session, with the group — Molinari, Kelsey Zozzaro, Anna Hele, and Kenny Leite — keeping Tristan company for roughly 40 minutes. The teens later said they had no idea Tristan had autism when they first invited him over; they just saw a kid sitting by himself and decided to change that. A separate video report from CBS News, with reporting from WBZ-TV's Paul Burton, featured Tristan's mother, Christina Caron, saying she felt he was included.

Tristan's mother, Christina Caron, was so moved by the gesture that she tracked the teenagers down on Facebook to thank them personally, turning a quiet afternoon at a trampoline park into a story that spread well beyond Milford and Bellingham. The two towns sit next to each other in south-central Massachusetts, and Urban Air functions as something of a regional hub for families in the area — the same CBS News Boston report notes that the park draws visitors from across the region, while Kids Out and About describes it as a primary indoor recreation destination pulling in families from Milford, Franklin, Hopkinton, and Woonsocket.

Once the story gained traction, Urban Air Adventure Park reached out to everyone involved and said it plans to invite the group back to the facility, per the same CBS News Boston account. The Bellingham park, located at 189 Mechanic Street, already runs a monthly Sensory Friendly Play session on the second Sunday of each month, according to Urban Air Adventure Park. Those sessions lower music volume and turn off strobe and flashing lights to better accommodate neurodivergent visitors.

Research helps explain why a casual invitation to play carries extra weight for a child like Tristan. Academic research published by the National Institutes of Health has found that children on the autism spectrum report higher rates of loneliness and engage in about half as much spontaneous peer social interaction as their neurotypical peers, underscoring the therapeutic value of exactly the kind of unplanned inclusion the Milford teens offered.

The interaction offers a personal example of inclusion for a child with autism.

The teenagers involved come from Milford, according to CBS Boston.

For now, the story remains a small but notable example of peer kindness rippling outward — from a trampoline park in Bellingham, to a mother's Facebook search, to a commercial venue planning to invite the group back.

packets.text:
A group of teenagers turned an ordinary day at an indoor adventure park into something extraordinary when they invited a 7-year-old boy with autism to join their fun, giving him a chance to feel included and his mother a memory she will never forget.
Christina and Tristan (left) reunite with the teenagers / CBS News
Christina Caron was visiting Urban Air Adventure Park in Bellingham, Massachusetts, with her son, Tristan, when a group of teens noticed him sitting by himself.
One of the teenagers, Livy Molinari, decided to strike up a conversation by complimenting a ball Tristan had just won.
"I said, 'That's a really nice ball you have,'" Livy recalled. She asked if she could hold it for a moment, and Tristan happily agreed. That simple exchange soon turned into an invitation to play.
Before long, the teens and Tristan were tossing the ball around, playing hide-and-seek and enjoying the slides together. What started as a casual interaction grew into about 40 minutes of laughter and fun.
And for Tristan's mom, watching it unfold meant more than the teenagers could have imagined. Christina explained that her son isn't always treated with the kindness and understanding he deserves.
"More often than not, he's not met with kindness," she said, explaining that children who are perceived as "a little bit different" aren't always met with understanding.
That's what made this moment so special. The teens didn't make a big deal out of Tristan being different. They simply saw a boy sitting alone and decided to make room for him.
Christina was deeply moved by their warmth and willingness to include her son.
"To see these teenagers just be so inclusive, and so welcoming and warm, it was just a really good feeling," she said.
"It was just a really good feeling to know that there are so many wonderful kids out there who are going to accept my son for the wonderful little boy and sweet boy that he is."
The teenagers later told WBZ-TV that they hadn't even known Tristan had autism. They weren't trying to make a statement or do anything extraordinary. They just wanted another kid to have fun with them.
"We just wanted to include him and have a fun time playing around at Urban Air," said Anna Hele, one of the teens. "And I feel really happy he felt included and as joyful as he did."
As word of the encounter spread online, the teenagers found themselves receiving attention for an act they had never expected to become a big story.
Kenny Leite, another member of the group, hopes their experience might inspire others to do the same.
"It's nice we included him and other people get to know about this, so maybe they can think about it when other people aren't included," he said.
That's perhaps the most important part of this story. Inclusion doesn't always require a grand gesture or a perfect understanding of someone else's life. Sometimes, it starts with noticing a person who is alone, saying hello and asking them to join in.
As Christina put it, "A small act of kindness can really turn someone's day around. It can change the trajectory, and it just meant so much to me."
For Tristan, it was 40 minutes of play with some new friends. For his mom, it was a powerful reminder that there are people who will see her son, welcome him and make sure he has a place to belong.

packets.text:
“More often than not, he’s not met with kindness,” Christina Caron said after a group of teenagers invited her 7-year-old son, Tristan, who has autism, to play with them at a Bellingham family entertainment center.

The encounter took place on a Monday at Urban Air Adventure Park in Bellingham, Massachusetts, CBS News reported. Caron was waiting in line to buy popcorn for Tristan when the group of teenagers walked up and asked him to join them. The teens played catch with Tristan and included him in a game of hide-and-seek.

For Caron, the experience stood out because her son often faces social exclusion. She noted that children perceived as different are sometimes viewed by others as a threat or simply as something unfamiliar.

“To see these teenagers just be so inclusive, and so welcoming and warm, it was just a really good feeling,” Caron said. She added that seeing young people accept Tristan for who he is provided deep reassurance.

Chad Darling, the owner of Urban Air Adventure Park, pointed out that the interaction highlights the positive connections that occur when young people reach out to strangers. Darling noted that the facility has operated for about eight years, making it a frequent backdrop for children making new friends.

Following the visit to the adventure park, Caron used Facebook to identify the teenagers involved in the game. She expressed her hope to connect directly with their parents to share how much the afternoon meant to her family.

Urban Air Adventure Park management has also reached out to Caron. The facility plans to invite everyone involved back to the park for a special day dedicated to celebrating the teenagers’ gesture.

“It just shows kids, teenagers, a small moment, anyone really, that a small moment, a small act of kindness can really turn someone’s day around,” Caron said. “It can change the trajectory, and it just meant so much to me.”
